This can take a significant amount time as it iterates along the constraints in an attempt to find a feasible solution. The dominate reason for being infeasible is the battery has insufficient capacity to provide power when needed along the route. As a result, we perform a pre-test on the power schedule sent to the lp to verify that there can be sufficient battery power. This is accomplished by evaluating the power requirements along the route and taking any excess power to recharge the batteries back to the maximum charge. If it is determined that there is insufficient battery storage, then the maximum speed is reduced iteratively until a solution can be found. Once this constraint has been satisfied, it is sent to the lp solver to calculate the optimal powering policy. In some highly underpowered consists, there is still not a solution and as a result, and failure message is returned to the user. The size of the lp problem can get quite large as the number of intervals being considered increases. It is common for there to be more than 10,000 intervals (this happens for most routes in excess of 500 miles). While the small segment lengths provide granularity to the analysis, for long routes the problem becomes computationally prohibitive. The size of the lp problem is reduced by recombining the analysis segments into chunks, which are contiguous groups segments that have the following common properties: • Battery is not required to meet the max propulsive power required • Battery is required to meet the max propulsive power required • Regenerative power is required • A number of segments in the chuck is exceeded (50 segments) Note that the algorithm treats the entire route at once, with energy requirements at the end of the route potentially impacting energy allocations at the beginning. This is in comparison to algorithms that use, for example, a finite time step look ahead, or even something more naïve such as a heuristic like use the cheapest fuel first, then the next, then the next. The E-LTD model also incorporates naïve powering policy heuristics in order to compare the optimal to the naïve. IV.Results The previously identified algorithms are implemented in the SCORE toolset. This is a web-based application for performing trade studies on alternative energy sources and current technologies for the Class 1 freight rail system. It provides the user with an intuitive graphical interface to select common routes, create and select consists, and select powering policies, variations of naïve or optimal. The selected simulation can be executed in the cloud and the results presented to the user in a number of summary and detailed plots and charts. The first result presented here is a comparison of the results from integrating the simulation using the distances versus a more traditional time based integration.
